name: The Roche Lobe
statement: Around each star in a pair is a teardrop of space it can hold; overflow it and matter spills to the other.
statementAccent: overflow it and matter spills to the other
meaning: The Roche lobe is the region around a star in a binary system within which orbiting material remains gravitationally bound to that star. In a pair of stars, each star has its own teardrop-shaped Roche lobe, and the two lobes meet at a single point between them, the inner Lagrange point L1, forming a figure-eight. Material inside a star's Roche lobe stays with that star, but if the star swells to fill and overflow its lobe, matter can spill through the L1 point onto the companion. This process, called Roche-lobe overflow, is the engine of mass transfer in interacting binary stars and drives some of the most dramatic phenomena in astrophysics, from accretion disks and novae to certain models of Type Ia supernovae. The Roche lobe is named after the French astronomer Édouard Roche, who lent his name to several related concepts. It is a distinct idea from the Roche limit, which concerns tidal breakup, and the Roche sphere, which concerns gravitational influence.
mechanism: The Roche lobe is defined by the gravitational and rotational forces in a binary system, viewed in the frame that rotates with the two stars. In that frame, the combined gravity of the two stars and the centrifugal effect of rotation define surfaces of constant effective potential. Close to each star the equipotential surfaces are nearly spherical and enclose material bound to that star; farther out they grow and distort until, at a critical value, the surface pinches into a figure-eight that touches itself at the inner Lagrange point L1. Each lobe of that figure-eight is a Roche lobe. As long as a star fits inside its lobe, its matter is held; but when a star evolves and expands, for instance into a giant, it can fill its lobe and push material to the L1 point, where the gravitational balance lets that matter flow across to the companion's lobe. The transferred gas, carrying angular momentum, typically spirals into an accretion disk around the receiving star, releasing energy and powering a range of luminous, sometimes explosive, phenomena.

examples.text: A star that expands to fill its Roche lobe spills matter through the inner Lagrange point L1 onto its companion, transferring mass.
In a cataclysmic variable, a white dwarf accretes matter from a Roche-lobe-filling companion, forming an accretion disk that can flare as a nova.

examples.tag: A route to Type Ia supernovae
examples.text: In one progenitor model, a white dwarf accreting from a Roche-lobe-filling companion nears the Chandrasekhar limit and detonates as a Type Ia supernova.

variants.name: Roche-lobe overflow
variants.text: The mass transfer that begins when a star fills and overflows its Roche lobe, spilling matter through L1 onto the companion.

variants.name: The critical equipotential
variants.text: The figure-eight surface, in the co-rotating frame, that pinches at L1 and bounds each star's Roche lobe.

whyItMatters: The Roche lobe is a central concept in the astrophysics of binary stars, because it determines when and how mass flows between two stars, a process that shapes their evolution and powers many of the most energetic phenomena in the sky. Roche-lobe overflow drives the mass transfer behind interacting binaries of all kinds: cataclysmic variables and novae, in which a white dwarf accretes from a companion; X-ray binaries and millisecond pulsars, where matter falls onto a neutron star or black hole; and, in one leading model, the Type Ia supernovae used as cosmic distance markers, where a white dwarf accretes toward the Chandrasekhar limit. The accretion disks that form from transferred matter are laboratories for high-energy astrophysics. By defining the boundary of gravitational binding for each star and the gateway between them at L1, the Roche lobe provides the geometric framework for understanding how binary stars exchange matter, evolve, and sometimes explode, making it indispensable to stellar astrophysics.

working.text: in the rotating frame of the binary, find the surfaces of constant effective potential shaped by both stars' gravity and rotation.
locate the figure-eight equipotential that pinches at the inner Lagrange point L1, bounding each star's Roche lobe.
when a star fills its lobe, let matter spill through L1 to the companion, forming an accretion disk and powering activity.

limits: The Roche lobe is defined within an idealized model, typically assuming two point-mass stars on a circular orbit and co-rotation, so real systems with eccentric orbits, non-synchronous rotation, or extended stars require refinements. The onset and rate of Roche-lobe overflow depend on the detailed structure and evolution of the donor star, which are complex. The Type Ia supernova connection is one progenitor channel, the single-degenerate model, and is thought to account for only a minority of such explosions, with white-dwarf mergers and other routes proposed for the rest, so it should not be presented as the sole mechanism. The Roche lobe must also be kept distinct from the Roche limit and Roche sphere, related but different concepts.
misreadings: The Roche lobe is not the same as the Roche limit; the lobe bounds gravitational binding in a binary, while the limit concerns tidal breakup of a body, two distinct Roche concepts. Overflow is not a gentle leak but the driver of dramatic mass transfer through L1 that can power novae and supernovae. And the Type Ia supernova route via Roche-lobe overflow is one model, not the only one, so treating the lobe as the Roche limit, or the single-degenerate channel as the sole cause of Type Ia supernovae, misreads a concept that defines the region of binding around each star in a binary.
origin: Named after the French astronomer Édouard Roche, who lent his name to several concepts; the region bound to each star in a binary, meeting at the inner Lagrange point, central to mass transfer.
